samf-senior-2004-r1-02.title: Estimate
samf-senior-2004-r1-02.body:
The tallest skyscrapers have over 100 storeys of 3 to 4 m each, so about $400$ m. Heights of $4$ m or $40$ m are those of houses and small buildings, and $4$ km or $40$ km are far too large.

**Answer: (A) 400 m**

samf-senior-2004-r1-03.title: Factor
samf-senior-2004-r1-03.body:
$111=3\times37$, so the numerator is $37(37+3)$ and the fraction equals $37+3=40$.

**Answer: (B) 40**

samf-senior-2004-r1-05.title: Radii
samf-senior-2004-r1-05.body:
The small square has side $2$, which is two radii, so the radius is $1$. The large square has side equal to four radii, $4$, hence area $16$.

**Answer: (A) 16**

samf-senior-2004-r1-06.title: Simplify step by step
samf-senior-2004-r1-06.body:
$\frac{1/2}{3/2}=\frac13$, so the numerator is $1-\frac13=\frac23$. $\frac{3/2}{1/2}=3$, so the denominator is $1+3=4$. Then $1-\frac{2/3}{4}=1-\frac16=\frac56$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac56$**

samf-senior-2004-r1-08.title: Work backwards
samf-senior-2004-r1-08.body:
Each term to the left is a difference: $p+0=1$ gives $p=1$; $n+p=0$ gives $n=-1$; $m+n=p$ gives $m=2$; $k+m=n$ gives $k=-3$.

**Answer: (C) $-3$**

samf-senior-2004-r1-10.title: Split the fraction
samf-senior-2004-r1-10.body:
$\frac{n+3}{n-1}=1+\frac4{n-1}$, so $n-1$ must be a divisor of $4$: $\pm1,\pm2,\pm4$. That gives six values of $n$: $2,0,3,-1,5,-3$.

**Answer: (B) 6**

samf-senior-2004-r1-12.title: Factorise
samf-senior-2004-r1-12.body:
If $p+1=k^2$ then $p=(k-1)(k+1)$. A prime has only the factors $1$ and $p$, so $k-1=1$, $k=2$, $p=3$. This is the only one.

**Answer: (A) 1**

samf-senior-2004-r1-13.title: Pair twos and fives
samf-senior-2004-r1-13.body:
$4^4=2^8$, so the product is $2^{10}\times3^3\times5^{11}=27\times5\times10^{10}=135\times10^{10}$. Its digits are $135$ followed by ten zeros, with digit sum $1+3+5=9$.

**Answer: (A) 9**

samf-senior-2004-r1-14.title: Compare areas
samf-senior-2004-r1-14.body:
Let $AB=b$ and the height be $h$; the area of $ABCD$ is $bh$. Triangle $AFN$ has area $\frac12\cdot\frac b2\cdot\frac h2=\frac18bh$. Triangle $NBC$ has area $\frac12\cdot\frac b2\cdot h=\frac14bh$. So $FNCD=bh-\frac18bh-\frac14bh=\frac58bh$ and the ratio is $\frac{1/8}{5/8}=\frac15$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac15$**

samf-senior-2004-r1-15.title: Count by length
samf-senior-2004-r1-15.body:
There is $1$ one-digit number (9), $10$ two-digit ($90$-$99$), $100$ three-digit, $1000$ four-digit and $10\,000$ five-digit numbers beginning with $9$. Total $1+10+100+1000+10000=11\,111$.

**Answer: (E) 11 111**

samf-senior-2004-r1-16.title: Inscribed angle
samf-senior-2004-r1-16.body:
The vertices lie on a circle, and side $EF$ subtends $360^\circ/9=40^\circ$ at the centre. The angle at the circumference ($A$) is half of that: $20^\circ$.

**Answer: (B) $20^\circ$**

samf-senior-2004-r1-17.title: Similar triangles
samf-senior-2004-r1-17.body:
Let the square have side $x$. The small white triangle at the top is similar to the whole triangle, so $\frac{b-x}{x}=\frac ba$, giving $x=\frac{ab}{a+b}$. The ratio is $\frac{x^2}{\frac12ab}=\frac{a^2b^2}{(a+b)^2}\cdot\frac{2}{ab}=\frac{2ab}{(a+b)^2}$.

**Answer: (D)**

samf-senior-2004-r1-19.title: Similar triangles
samf-senior-2004-r1-19.body:
$BC=2a$ and $AC=\sqrt{4a^2-1}$. Right triangles $CMP$ and $CAB$ share the angle at $C$, so $\frac{MP}{MC}=\frac{AB}{AC}$, giving $MP=\frac{a\cdot1}{\sqrt{4a^2-1}}$.

**Answer: (D)**

samf-senior-2004-r1-20.title: Tangent lengths
samf-senior-2004-r1-20.body:
Label the triangle $ABC$ with the right angle at $B$, so $AC=\sqrt2$. Let $O$ be the centre of the semicircle (on $AB$) and $P$ the point of tangency on $AC$. Then $OP\perp AC$ and $OP=OB=r$; the tangents from $C$ are equal: $PC=BC=1$. Triangle $APO$ is an isosceles right triangle, so $AP=OP=r$ and $AP+PC=AC$ gives $r+1=\sqrt2$, $r=\sqrt2-1$.

**Answer: (E) $\sqrt2-1$**

samf-senior-2004-r1-20.title: Coordinates
samf-senior-2004-r1-20.body:
Place the right angle at the origin with the centre $(0,r)$ on the vertical leg. The hypotenuse is $x+y=1$, whose distance from the centre is $\frac{1-r}{\sqrt2}$. Setting this equal to $r$: $1-r=r\sqrt2$, so $r=\frac1{1+\sqrt2}=\sqrt2-1$.

**Answer: (E) $\sqrt2-1$**
